Polarizers and Bridgers Simulation Replay

How to read this

Every column, color, shape, and toggle below encodes something specific. Expand any section for detail.

The three conditions & matched runs

Each numbered run in the Matched run dropdown (0001, 0002, 0003) is a matched triple: the same baseline population — drawn from real ANES 2024 survey respondents — the same seeded starting network, and the same order of discussion topics, replayed once under each of the three conditions below it. The only intentional difference between the three columns is which condition that population experienced.

  • Control — the unmodified population, no intervention.
  • Polarizers — two slots (one Democrat, one Republican) replaced with purpose-built polarizing agents, present from round 1.
  • Bridger — same as Polarizers, plus an 11th “Neutral” agent whose job is to build bridging ties through engagement, also present from round 1.
The round scrubber

Round 0 is the baseline: the randomly seeded starting network, plus every organic agent's opinions freshly elicited from the LLM before any discussion — not their raw human survey answer, so later “change” isn't confounded with how the model's persona differs from the real respondent.

Rounds 1–6 are the six discussion iterations, one per ANES issue topic, always in the same order across all three conditions in a matched triple — so topic is never confounded with condition.

The discussion panel

Full speech-bubble rows are POST/RESPOND — real generated text. Compact single-line rows are every other action an agent could take that round — liked, disliked, followed, unfollowed, or took no action — shown inline in the order they actually happened, not summarized away.

Reading agent color & shape

The same encoding applies to the discussion panel's avatars and the network graph's nodes. Column headers and the attention-list cards below use it too, just on text rather than a shape, since there's no avatar there to color.

  • Circle = an ordinary (“organic”) participant. Blue = Democrat, red = Republican. Shade tracks that agent's current in-party warmth (their own feeling-thermometer reading toward their own party) as of the round you're viewing — a live value, so a node can visibly darken or lighten round to round.
  • Triangle = a polarizer. Same blue/red party hue and shading rule as a circle, at the default mid-tone — being purpose-built, not a real survey respondent, they never get a warmth reading to shade by, so they stay fixed at that mid-tone rather than animating like an organic agent's. Shape, not color, is what marks them as a polarizer.
  • Purple triangle = the bridger. Flat purple always, since it isn't a partisan.
The network panel & the Follow/Interaction toggle

A force-directed graph of ties among that round's agents. Arrows show direction — who followed or engaged whom, not a symmetric line — and when two agents' ties run both directions you'll see two parallel arrows rather than one (roughly a quarter of ties in a typical round are reciprocal).

Follow shows persistent “who follows whom” ties. At round 0 this is the only real structure that exists — a random, homophily-weighted seeding before any discussion — which is why Follow is the default there. Follow ties don't fade on their own; they only change via explicit follow/unfollow actions, and agents rarely take those — across every committed run, follow/unfollow actions are far rarer than replies, likes, and dislikes, so the Follow view can look identical for rounds at a stretch. That's real agent behavior, not a stuck display.

For readers who want the generative model: round 0's seeding is a two-block Erdős–Rényi-style random directed graph. Every ordered pair of agents present at round 0 (polarizers included — they already hold their slots by then; the bridger is deliberately excluded, joining later with zero ties) gets an independent Bernoulli draw for a directed tie, at rate p = edge_probability + homophily_bonus for same-party pairs and p = edge_probability for cross-party pairs (both capped at 1). These demo runs use edge_probability = 0.25, homophily_bonus = 0.15 — a 40% same-party vs. 25% cross-party tie rate, i.e. same-party ties are 1.6× as likely. The draw uses its own RNG stream keyed to the run's seed, independent of every other random draw in the run (topic order, engagement order, condition assignment), so the starting topology comes out identical across all three conditions in a matched triple.

Interaction shows who has actually replied to, liked, or disliked whom, accumulated round over round. This is where the bridger's story shows up: it starts with zero ties of either kind and is meant to build them by engaging, so it can look isolated under Follow well past round 0 — which is why Interaction is the default from round 1 on.

The count next to NETWORK always reports how many ties are showing and how many more exist under the other mode, so a disconnected-looking node is never a silent mystery.

The outcomes strip

Split into two groups by where the number comes from — a distinction worth keeping straight, since they can disagree — and within each group, two rows: a trajectory across rounds (top), then a cross-condition bar comparison with 95% confidence intervals (bottom). The bar row tracks the same round scrubber as everything else on the page — it's not pinned to the final round, so scrub back to see how the comparison (and its uncertainty) looked earlier in the run. Line-chart condition is distinguished by color and style (solid teal Control, dashed amber Polarizers, dotted purple Bridger) — not by the red/blue/purple used for party, which is already spoken for elsewhere. The thin grey vertical line on trajectory charts marks whichever round the scrubber is on.

Survey-based — from OPINION_UPDATE, i.e. what an agent says when re-asked the ANES questions after the discussion. What agents report, not what they did.

  • On-topic issue polarization — mean(position | R) − mean(position | D) on whichever single ANES issue was that round's actual discussion topic, not averaged across all six items (five of which weren't even discussed that round). A demo-only variant showing the direct effect of that round's discussion.
  • Full-topic issue polarization — the same distance, but averaged across all six ANES items regardless of that round's topic. This is the quantity closest to the study's actual preregistered H1a DV.
  • Affective polarization — each organic agent's in-party feeling-thermometer warmth minus their out-party warmth, averaged across agents — the H1b proxy.

The bottom row repeats the same three, but as a bar per condition — and unlike everything else on this page, these three bars are static, not round-scrubber-dependent: each pools every organic agent's reading from all six discussion rounds (round 0 excluded — it has no topic yet), not just whichever round you're on. That trades round-by-round movement for a steadier estimate off a larger effective sample (up to 24–30 agent-round observations per party per condition instead of 4–5 agents). The 95% confidence interval is computed the same way as before (a t-distribution critical value, not the z=1.96 shortcut): for the two distance bars it combines each party group's own uncertainty (their means' standard errors, combined); for affective polarization it's the standard error of the pooled agent-level gap. On the Pooled tab, this pooling stacks on top of the existing seed-pooling — all three matched seeds' agents across all six rounds, combined into one number per condition.

Behavior-based — from what actually happened in the room: replies, likes, dislikes, follows. What agents did, not what they said afterward.

  • Likes & follows / Dislikes & unfollows / Responses — each card splits into two small side-by-side charts, cross-party and within-party, each comparing the three conditions the normal way (solid/dashed/dotted by color). Worth knowing going in: LIKE is essentially always same-party across every committed run (a real ceiling effect, not a rendering issue — the within-party mini-chart moves, the cross-party one barely does), while RESPOND skews the opposite way — agents mostly reply to rebut people they disagree with, not to agree with people they don't.
  • Cross-party edge ratio — the share of all current ties (follow and interaction combined, regardless of which the toggle above the network panel is currently showing) that connect a Democrat to a Republican. A raw count-based ratio, not adjusted for how many D vs. R nodes exist to connect to.
  • Most attention received — per condition, the top 3 by incoming RESPOND/LIKE/DISLIKE/FOLLOW/UNFOLLOW count (every action with a real target, i.e. every event type except POST and DO_NOTHING), tallied cumulatively from round 1 through whichever round the scrubber is on — positive and negative attention both count here. Tracks the scrubber like everything else here, so the ranking can reshuffle as a run plays out. On Replay, ranked by individual agent (A5, A9, …), text colored the same way as agent color elsewhere (party hue, live warmth where it exists); on Pooled, individual IDs aren't comparable across seeds, so it's ranked by the same five identity categories used everywhere else on the page instead — D organic, R organic, D Polarizer, R Polarizer, Bridger, each colored the same way — summed across all three seeds' timelines (see the Pooled tab note below).
  • Most positive attention received — the same idea, restricted to LIKE/FOLLOW (always positive by construction) plus only the RESPONDs that read as agreement. There's no sentiment field on RESPOND, so agreement is detected with a small lexical heuristic — phrases like “you're right,” “I agree,” “well said” anywhere in the message. It's not a real classifier: it will miss agreement phrased less directly, so this undercounts positive RESPOND rather than overcounts it. Given RESPOND otherwise skews heavily toward rebuttal (see above), that undercounting bias is the safer direction to err in.

All of this is descriptive from these specific demo runs — the Replay tab is one matched triple per seed, not a confirmatory statistical result. The Pooled tab (below) widens the sample by combining every matched seed, which is where these confidence intervals get more meaningful.

Opinion distributions

Below the outcomes strip: for a chosen measure, the actual spread of organic agents' values, not just a mean — a kernel density estimate (a smoothed histogram) per party, per condition. Outline = round 0, before any discussion. Filled = the round the scrubber is currently on. The dots on the baseline are each curve's mean; hollow = round-0 mean, filled = current-round mean, and the text under each chart spells out that same before → after (delta) reading.

Four measures, selected with the buttons above the charts:

  • On-topic issue — whichever ANES issue the round you're viewing is discussing. The baseline curve isn't round 0's own topic (round 0 has none) — it's that same issue's value as measured at round 0, before it was ever discussed. So this is a genuine before/after-that-specific-discussion comparison, not before/after the whole run.
  • All issues (mean) — each agent's mean across all six ANES items, round 0 vs. the current round.
  • Warmth toward Dem. / Rep. — the feeling-thermometer readings themselves (not the animosity gap), split by the agent's own party, so you can see e.g. how Republicans' warmth toward Democrats shifts independent of how Democrats feel about themselves.

With only 4–5 organic agents per party per condition in these demo runs, treat the curve shapes as illustrative, not a real density estimate — the means and the before/after deltas are the more trustworthy read at this sample size.

The Pooled tab

No discussion panel and no network graph — there's no single conversation to replay once you combine seeds whose actual discussions differed. Instead, every organic agent from all three matched runs (0001, 0002, 0003) is pooled together at each round index, giving the same outcomes-strip and distributions views as Replay, just over roughly 3× the sample (24–30 organic agents per party per condition instead of 4–5) — which is where the 95%-CI bars start to mean more. The two attention cards still read the raw event timeline (it isn't part of the pooled agent/round data), so they reach across all three seeds' timelines directly and rank by identity category instead of individual agent, per the note above.

Pooling works even though each seed randomizes its own topic order independently: on-topic values are pooled at the value level (this round's reading, whatever issue it happened to be, from whichever seed), not by matching topics across seeds — see the on-topic issue distance/polarization entries above. The round scrubber is shared with the Replay tab, so switching tabs keeps your position.
